binders: A finite index type iota and a measurable outcome space Omega.
A probability measure mu on Omega.
A finite family W_i : Omega -> R indexed by iota.
hypotheses: The family (W_i) is mutually independent under mu.
For every i, W_i(omega) belongs to [0,1] for mu-almost every omega.
For every i, the expectation integral_mu W_i is at most 1/2 - delta.
The family size N = card(iota) is positive.
N, viewed as a real number, is at least log(1/epsilon)/(2 delta^2).
conclusions: The real-valued mu-measure of the event {omega : sum_i W_i(omega) >= N/2} is at most epsilon.
mathematical_definitions: N denotes the finite cardinality of iota.
The expectation of W_i is its real Bochner integral with respect to mu.
The probability in the conclusion is Measure.real, i.e. the extended-nonnegative measure of the event converted to a real number.
The sum is taken over all indices in iota.
translation.proposition_plain_english: Let (W_i) be a nonempty finite family of mutually independent measurable real random variables on a probability space. Suppose each W_i lies between 0 and 1 almost surely and has expectation at most 1/2 - delta, where delta > 0. For any epsilon with 0 < epsilon < 1, if the family size N satisfies N >= log(1/epsilon)/(2 delta^2), then the probability that the total sum of the W_i is at least N/2 is at most epsilon.

restrictions_and_vacuity_risks: The index set must be finite and explicitly nonempty.
The theorem concerns arbitrary independent [0,1]-valued random variables, not necessarily identically distributed, Bernoulli-valued, or integer-valued.
Only an upper bound on each expectation is assumed; no equality or common distribution is required.
The conclusion uses the non-strict threshold sum_i W_i >= N/2 and a non-strict probability bound <= epsilon.

Because every W_i is nonnegative almost surely on a probability space, the hypotheses become inconsistent when 1/2 - delta is negative; thus choices delta > 1/2 create a vacuous regime for the required nonempty family.
The sample-size lower bound is a real inequality involving the exact finite cardinality; there is no explicit ceiling operation.
The probability is represented by conversion of an extended-nonnegative measure to a real; in this probability-measure setting the event has finite measure.
